standard.breakdownMd:
**Facts**

Some med students and a doctor are looking at a sick patient trying to diagnose.

The doctor says, "Meg, what tests would we order to rule out lupus? Tony, what would we order to rule out emphysema? Karthik, what would we order to rule out diabetes?"

A week later these same med students and a different doctor are looking at a similar sick patient.

The new doctor says, "Well, how would we diagnose this patient?"
Meg says, "here's how I would rule out lupus ..."
Tony says, "here's how I would rule out emphysema ... "

**Evaluate**

This one seems to be like a Solve the Causal Mystery / Identify the Causal Difference-Maker type setup. We have some interesting behavior in that each med student is going back to the disease they were asked about initially.

Can we say something safely worded like, "When you're asked to rule out a diagnosis, you're more likely to think of that diagnosis?", or "Being asked by an authority figure about a certain topic makes that topic stand out in your mind relative to other similar topics?"

**Goal**

Pick the most provable answer (it might be a safely worded explanation for why the med students are going back to their original diagnosis).

A.text: On the second occasion, none of the medical students began by testing the same diagnosis as any of the other medical students.
A.explanation: This seems pretty provable. Since they were all given different diseases the first time (one got X, one got Y, one got Z), and since they all began the second time by addressing the disease they were given (one began with X, one began with Y, one began with Z), it seems pretty safe to say that none of them began in the same way.

B.text: At most one of the medical students knew which of the several medical conditions was most likely to lead to the patients' symptoms.
B.tag: Out of Scope: knew the most likely one
B.explanation:
This tries to make an inference from the inference. Since they all began by talking about different diagnoses, at most one of them was correct?

Two problems:
- it's possible that more than one condition afflicts the patient. It might be a combo of diabetes and emphysema.
- it's possible that the med students began talking about the disease assigned to them in the first go-round, even though the student knew a different medical condition was more likely to lead to those symptoms.

We'd be making a leap from "if you started by talking about disease X, then you thought that X was most likely to lead to the patients' symptoms", but that's not a definite move we can make.

C.text: The second attending physician was unaware of the results of the students' encounter with the first attending physician.
C.explanation:
We have no idea whether the second doctor was in on this scheme or oblivious to it. She just asked the students, "What do y'all think is the diagnosis?"

That's compatible with her being aware of what the first doctor did or being oblivious to it.

D.text: On the second occasion, exactly one of the students tested for the medical condition that actually caused the patient's symptoms.
D.explanation:
This is like (B) in trying to go one step farther ... "Since they all tested for different diseases, only one of them was right."

Two problems:
- more than one condition might afflict the patient, so more than one student can be right
- it might be that all the students were wrong, so maybe zero students were testing for the correct condition(s)

E.text: At least some of the medical students were unaware that the patients' symptoms could be the result of medical conditions other than the one suggested by the original attending physician.
E.explanation:
We can't speak to what the med students were or weren't aware of. We didn't get any information about their thoughts.

Their behavior in repeating the disease they were assigned the first time around could mean that they think "one of those conditions the first doctor offered must have been the right answer", but it could also mean "the doctors want me to prove that I can rule out all these wrong answers first".

---

standard.breakdownMd:
**Conclusion**

Caffeine consumption is the main reason that teenagers who consume caffeinated sodas have a higher incidence of broken bones.

**Evidence**

Caffeinated sodas cause people to excrete more calcium. Calcium deficiency can make bones more brittle (presumably making them easier to break).

**Evaluate**

This is the classic Curious Fact / Explanation template we expect on lots of Strengthen / Weaken questions.

Curious Fact: Why do teenagers who drink caffeinated sodas have a higher incidence of broken bones?

Author's Story: The caffeinated soda drains their calcium, leading to calcium deficiency, leading to brittle bones, leading to more easily broken bones.

We always address these with the same two pressure points:
- Is there some OTHER STORY that could explain the Curious Fact?
- How plausible is the AUTHOR'S STORY?

**Goal**

Since this is Weaken, we know to prioritize thinking about OTHER STORIES.

How else could we explain the correlation between caffeinated soda and broken bones? Our customary go-to alternative explanations for correlations are Reverse Causality and Third Factor.

Could it be that breaking bones came first and caffeinated sodas came next? Maybe. Unlikely, but maybe teens who break their bones become sedentary and sleepier and start drinking caffeinated sodas more to pep themselves up.

Could there be some Third Factor that really caused the broken bones and just happens to go along with the caffeinated sodas? Sure, there's the whole Mountain Dew X-Games angle. The kids most likely to drink caffeinated sodas are the ones who most frequently engage in physically dangerous activities like skateboarding / snowboarding.

On a first pass prioritize looking for a different Causal Story, but we could also use an answer that disrupts the plausibility of the author's storyline: first they drank caffeinated soda, then calcium deficiency, then brittle bones.

A.text: Teenagers who drink large quantities of carbonated beverages containing caffeine tend to drink smaller quantities of calcium-rich beverages than other teenagers do.
A.explanation:
This gives us a Third Factor alternate explanation.

It's not the caffeinated soda that's causing these teens to have lower calcium and more brittle bones than their peers, it's the fact that they drink smaller quantities of calcium-rich beverages.

You have teens drinking Mountain Dew, and other teens drinking milk. This answer is saying that the primary reason the Mountain Dew kids have more broken bones isn't that their MTN Dew drains their calcium but rather that they didn't have a milk-boosted supply of calcium to start with.

Technically, we know the caffeinated soda drinking still contributes to lower calcium, but we now have a way to argue it's not the primary reason for their broken bones.

B.text: Teenagers engage in the types of activities that carry a high risk of causing broken bones much more often than both older and younger people do.
B.explanation: For this to be out answer it would need to say "Teenagers who drink caffeinated sodas engage in more broken bone activities than those who don't."

C.text: Some teenagers have calcium deficiencies even though they do not consume any caffeine.
C.explanation:
The word "some" is wrong at least 90% of the time you see it in Strengthen, Weaken, Paradox since it's so weak.

This says that there is at least one teenager who has a calcium deficiency even though they don't drink coffee. Cool. His name is Jeff, and he's sitting right here. "Sorry, Jeff, but you're irrelevant to this argument".

Arguments about correlations and averages leave plenty of room for exceptions, but LSAT always writes this type of trap answer to bait people into objecting, "But that's not true 100% of the time!" You're right, but the author agrees with you. The author never said it was 100% of the time.

D.text: Some of the less popular carbonated beverages contain even more caffeine than the more popular ones.
D.explanation:
This is again super dubious given that it says "Some". There's no impact on this argument by saying, "There is at least one less popular caffeinated soda that has even more caffeine than more popular ones".

How does that help us argue that caffeinated soda is not the primary reason that teens who drink caffeinated have a higher rate of broken bones?

Saying that "some brands have even more caffeine" doesn't allow us to think "oh, the brands that the teens are drinking don't REALLY have caffeine".

E.text: The more calcium a person ingests as a regular part of his or her diet, the more calcium that person will tend to excrete.
E.explanation:
The more water I drink, the more I'll pee. What does this have to do with assessing the putative causal connection between caffeinated soda and broken bones?

The people who make more money, spend more money, but they still end up with more money than the person who was low on money to begin with.

So people who eat more calcium excrete more calcium, but still end up being someone with higher calcium (we assume).

---

standard.breakdownMd:
**Main Conclusion**

If you're trying to praise or blame a group, you need to cast that statement in terms of individuals, if we're gonna properly evaluate your claim.

**Intermediate Conclusion**

Groups are not a type of entity that you can praise or blame.

**Evidence**

Blaming something requires that the thing has conscience and agency (an ability to decide for themselves).

Nations don't have consciences. Families are not agents.

**Evaluate**

On Role questions, it's unusual for the last claim of the paragraph to be the Main Conclusion (only about 10% of the time), but we know it's a conclusion from the fact that it's prefaced by Hence.

On Role questions, it's very common for the first claim of the paragraph to be the Main Conclusion, and the first claim of this paragraph is a conclusion, since we immediately start unpacking / supporting it with the 2nd and 3rd sentences.

To figure out the relationship between those two conclusions (the first and last claim) we can use the Support Test. Which one would be a supporting idea for the other?

why should we believe that groups aren't the sort of entity you can praise/blame?

why should we believe that if we want to praise or blame a group, we have to translate that into a statement about individuals, or else we can't evaluate it properly?

When we ask the 2nd question, the 1st claim actually sounds like Support.

Why should we re-cast praise or blame about a group into statements about individuals? Because, groups aren't the sort of entity you can praise or blame.

This is how we know the first claim is subordinate to the last claim.

**Goal**

We're being asked about the 3rd sentence, which was a premise. If we wanted to get more specific, it was a premise helping to support the Intermediate Conclusion.

A.text: It is an intermediate conclusion offered as direct support for the argument's main conclusion.
A.explanation:
To test whether something is an Intermediate Conclusion, just ask yourself, "Why should I believe this?"

If you can point to any claim in the argument and say, "because, [this claim]", then the claim you were testing was a conclusion. If you can't find a supporting claim, it's not a conclusion.

Why should I believe that ... nations do not have consciences?

There isn't any premise offered for that.

B.text: It is offered as support for an intermediate conclusion that is in turn offered as direct support for the argument's main conclusion.
B.explanation:
The 2nd, 3rd, and 4th sentences combine to flow into the 1st sentence.

- If something doesn't have a conscience or doesn't have agency, then it can't be blamed.
- Nations don't have consciences (can't be blamed).
- Family are not agents (can't be blamed).

Thus
- Groups (like nations and families) aren't the sort of thing that can be praised or blamed.

Hence
- If we're trying to praise a blame a group, we better translate that into praise or blame for individuals.

C.text: It is cited as an implication of the main conclusion drawn in the argument.
C.explanation:
The main conclusion is an implication of the Intermediate Conclusion, which is an implication of the premises. And the claim we're being asked about is a Premise.

The verb "implies" is the same as the → of reasoning.

Premise —implies→ Conclusion.

D.text: It is cited as an instance of a general conclusion drawn in the argument.
D.explanation:
"An instance of a general claim" is the same as an example of a general claim.

We did have two general conclusions drawn within the argument:

Intermed Conc: groups aren't the sort of entity that can be praised or blamed.

An instance of that would sound like "for instance, nations can't be praised or blamed. Families can't be praised or blamed."

Main Conc: praise or blame for a group should be translated into statements about individuals.

An instance of that would be like, "for instance, if you're trying to praise New Zealand for its handling of COVID, you should really name specific individuals that deserve praise."

E.text: It is the main conclusion drawn in the argument.
E.explanation:
The final claim is the main conclusion.

The 2nd, 3rd, and 4th sentences combine to flow into the 1st sentence.

- If something doesn't have a conscience or doesn't have agency, then it can't be blamed.
- Nations don't have consciences (can't be blamed).
- Family are not agents (can't be blamed).

Thus
- Groups (like nations and families) aren't the sort of thing that can be praised or blamed.

Hence
- If we're trying to praise a blame a group, we better translate that into praise or blame for individuals.

---

standard.breakdownMd:
**Conclusion**

Overcoming negative emotions could cause one's health to improve.

**Evidence**

Psychological stress is known both to cause negative emotions and to impair physical health.

**Evaluate**

Normally, when we see a causal conclusion, there was a correlation between X and Y in the evidence. The author overconfidently concludes that X causes Y, and we consider alternate explanations such as,
- Reverse Causality (maybe Y causes X?)
- Third Factor (maybe X and Y are both caused by Z?)

In this argument, though, the evidence also had a causal claim. It's almost as though this argument started by establishing that there is a Third Factor, Z, psychological stress, that causes X and Y (negative emotions and impaired physical health).

The author bizarrely assumes that X causes Y, out of this love triangle.

**Goal**

We could point out that the author's thinking, "If two things are both effects of the same cause, one of those thing is causing the other thing."

We could raise an objection that, "even if X and Y are both symptoms of underlying condition Z, changing X might have no effect on Y."

A.text: It presumes without justification that two conditions that together have a certain effect causally influence one another.
A.explanation:
This is very close, but the two conditions (negative emotions and impaired physical health) are not conditions that together have a certain effect. Instead, they are both effects of the same cause.

This answer is saying "since negative emotions combined with bad health, often result in psychological stress, overcoming negative emotions could cause improved health."

B.text: It presumes, merely on the basis that two conditions have a common cause, that one of these two conditions can causally influence the other.
B.explanation:
Any answer structured, "Presumes, merely on the basis of X, that Y", makes us check whether X matches the evidence and Y matches the conclusion.

Was the premise that two conditions have a common cause?

Yes. Negative emotions and bad physical health are both caused by psychological stress.

Does the conclusion act like one of those two conditions can causally influence the other?

Yes. The conclusion says that getting rid of negative emotions could cause one's health to improve.

C.text: It confuses two causes that together are necessary to bring about an effect with causes that are sufficient for that effect.
C.explanation:
When we see "necessary", "sufficient", or any synonyms for those ideas, they're talking about the famous Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw, which is when the author presents a conditional statement in the premise and then applies it in some illegal Backwards or Opposite fashion to derive her conclusion.

Any time we see this answer choice, we should just ask ourselves, "Was there any conditional logic?"

If not, it's wrong. If so, it's right 95% of the time. There was no conditional logic in this paragraph.

D.text: It takes for granted that two conditions that together have a certain effect can, each by itself, produce the same effect.
D.explanation:
This breaks for the same initial reason that (A) did. Do we have two conditions that together have a certain effect?

Nope. Negative emotions and impaired physical health are not conditions that together have a certain effect. Instead, they are both effects of the same cause.

The second half of this answer is also a mismatch, but we needn't read that far to get rid of it.

E.text: It takes for granted that removing a condition that causally contributes to another condition suffices to eliminate the latter condition.
E.explanation:
Saying that "the author takes for granted that X suffices to do Y" makes it seem like X should match evidence and Y should match conclusion.

The conclusion is saying that removing the condition of negative emotions could cause one's health to improve. It never says "it suffices (guarantees)" to eliminate the latter condition.

---

standard.breakdownMd:
**Statements**

As we search for Causal, Conditional, Comparative, or Pivot type wording, we see two causal claims.

- causal (work by): Some anticancer drugs work by depriving growing tumors of needed blood vessels.
- causal (work by): These drugs inhibit the process of angiogenesis, which is the creation of new blood vessels.
- causal (prevent): The same drugs prevent obesity.

**Evaluate**

They tell us the causal mechanism by which anticancer drugs work, inhibiting the creation of new blood vessels (angiogenesis), and then they tell us that the same drugs prevent obesity in rodents.

So it seems like the synthesis we could get here is that the same causal mechanism somehow prevents obesity.

**Goal**

If we were to try to use what we learned from the first two sentences with what we're told in the last sentence, we would probably be saying something like, "inhibiting the creation of new blood vessels (angiogenesis) prevents obesity in rats".

A.text: The cells in tumors are more similar in structure to fat cells than to other cells in the body.
A.explanation:
We know that both tumors and obesity are thwarted by inhibiting angiogenesis, but that doesn't mean that tumor cells and fat cells are closer to each other than to other types of cells in the body.

We have no means of comparing them to other cells in the body.

B.text: Drugs that inhibit angiogenesis would probably enable obese humans to lose weight.
B.explanation:
This is a very tempting answer, since it reinforces our prediction that "inhibiting angiogenesis prevents obesity in rodents".

But preventing obesity is a very different concept from losing weight (reversing obesity).

Sunscreen prevents me from getting a sunburn, but if I'm already sunburnt, applying sunscreen doesn't help me to lose the sunburn.

C.text: Fat tissue depends on angiogenesis in order to grow.
C.explanation:
This reinforces our prediction that "inhibiting angiogenesis prevents obesity in rats".

Now, are there problems with this correct answer? Oh my heavens, yes.
1. depends is very strong

However, we were told that tumors need these blood vessels to be created and that this drug prevents cancer from spreading by denying them their needed blood vessels. Since we're saying the same drug (that inhibits angiogenesis) works to prevent obesity, it's reasonable to think that fat cells also need / depend on blood vessels.

2. Fat tissue? Where did that come from?

Well, naturally it relates to obesity, but it sounds overly specific. It also might concern people that they're using outside knowledge when it comes to connecting obesity with fat tissue. You're allowed to use common sense knowledge. If you asked 10 people on the street whether obesity was connected to fat, they'd probably all say yes.

Is is common sense that obesity involves the growth of fat tissue? Hmm, pretty close. I think idiots like me wouldn't have ever defined obesity that way, because we're not smart enough about biology to think to use the term fat tissue, but if you asked me if someone who was becoming obese or more obese was gaining fat tissue, I would say, "yeah, right?"

3. Isn't this too broad? We only should be able to say "fat tissue in rodents depends on angiogenesis".

Sure, we were only told about rodents, but it's common sense that lots of testing of products and medicines happens on rodents before it's used on humans, since rodents are also mammals and our physiology is apparently similar enough that what we learn from testing rodents usually ports over pretty well to humans too. (Guinea pigs are rodents, and we probably all know the expression of "I don't want to be the guinea pig" means "I don't want to be the test subject")

4. Jeez, Patrick, if you have to itemize multiple possible qualms and then kinda make peace with each one, doesn't that add up to a pretty poorly supported answer?

Yes, kind of. But is there a more supported answer? This question stem tolerates fuzzy support, if no other answer has clearer support.

D.text: Rodents with cancer are more likely to be obese than healthy rodents.
D.tag: Out of Scope: rodents with cancer / Unsupported Comparison
D.explanation:
We have no way to say that rodents with cancer are more obese than healthy rodents. This answer seems to want to bait people into thinking, "If you took drug X, it would get rid of your obesity and your cancer, so I guess that means the rodents with cancer haven't taken the drug and are still obese".

But there isn't any sense in which this drug has been distributed to rodents across the world. The obesity drug has been administered to a handful of rodents in an experimental setting (we have no idea whether those rodents did / didn't have cancer).

This answer is addressing all the rodents in the world with cancer, a group we know nothing about.

E.text: Drugs that inhibit angiogenesis also prevent absorption of vital nutrients.
E.explanation:
Nothing in this paragraph says anything about absorbing vital nutrients. This answer wants people to make an unsupported link from "If it prevents obesity, then it prevents you from absorbing vital nutrients".

---

standard.breakdownMd:
**Conclusion**

It's pointless trying to spend too much time trying to perfectly match your new shade of paint to the old shade (if you're doing touch-ups)

**Evidence**

The color of all paint fades and changes within about a year of being on the wall, so even if you nail the matching shade of paint initially, it will still drift from that shade and eventually not match the old paint.

**Evaluate**

Since there was no conditional logic or quantifiers in this argument, it's probably not worth putting into algebra.

Let's just try to remove the topic and tell the same story:

- Premise 1: You want to find the perfect match/solution.
- Premise 2: But anything that would initially be perfect would eventually drift and no longer be perfect.
- Conclusion: Thus, it's pointless to spend too much energy trying to find the perfect match/solution.

**Goal**

The conclusion has a signature strength/type we might be able to use for some quick eliminations.

The conclusion on the correct answer should sound pretty dismissive of a certain strategy "it would be pointless to do X".

The problem with the strategy needs to feel something like "even if it starts off right, it'll become wrong".

A.text: A bicycle is most comfortable to ride when the wheels are perfectly aligned. However, because the position of a bike wheel always shifts a bit when the bike is ridden, it is useless to put very much effort into perfectly aligning a new wheel.
A.explanation: The conclusion is saying that a certain effort at perfection would be pointless (it's useless), based on the fact that even if it starts off right, it will inevitably drift away from perfection (always shifts a bit when ridden).

B.text: It is rarely worthwhile to look for parts for an older car. Because most cars do not last more than 20 years, it is best to buy a new car instead of restoring an older car.
B.tag: Weak Conclusion Match / Bad Premise Match
B.explanation:
We could already start distancing ourselves from this with the conclusion's "rarely worthwhile" strength. We're trying to match a conclusion that is more like "never worthwhile".

Also, the Premise doesn't have anything to do with "even if you nail it at first, it'll drift away from perfection".

C.text: Keeping hair healthy requires using a shampoo designed specifically for one's hair type. However, hair will become unhealthy if washed consistently with the same brand of shampoo. Thus, to maintain healthy hair, a person should alternate between two suitable shampoos.
C.explanation:
We'd save ourselves time and brainpower by checking the conclusion first and seeing that "you should alternate between A and B" is a terrible match for the original's "it is pointless to do A".

The premises here have a little bit of "drift from perfection" in them, but there's no point in trying to even make it work when the conclusion makes it dead on arrival.

D.text: Although cookies made with butter have a better texture than do cookies made with margarine, it is pointless to spend the extra money needed to buy butter, when cookies made with margarine are almost as good.
D.explanation:
The conclusion is definitely saying that a certain strategy is pointless.

Is the evidence saying "even if you start out perfect, you'll drift away from perfection"?

No, it's saying "an inferior but easier to acquire alternative is close enough that you might as well just go with that".

E.text: Unless the size and shape of a dress exactly matches the size and shape of its lining, the dress will hang unevenly when it is worn. However, because most people would not notice this unevenness, it is not worthwhile when making a dress to spend much time attempting to match a dress and its lining perfectly.
E.explanation:
The conclusion does say a certain strategy would be pointless.

Does the evidence say that "even if you nail it at first, you'll eventually drift from perfection"?

No, it says "almost no one will notice an imperfect attempt, so why bother".

---

standard.breakdownMd:
**Conclusion**

If ad agencies gear their ads mainly to older adults, they can maximize clients' profits.

**Evidence**

Older adults control more of this nation's personal disposable income than does the rest of the population combined.

**Evaluate**

If this were anything other than Sufficient Assumption, I would be tempted to start marshaling counterarguments, like "yes, but ... older people's consumer habits are already stuck, so ads don't make as much different", or "most of the money they spend is on behalf of other people, so ads should target those people".

But Sufficient Assumption just needs a math-y connector that adds on to what we're told in the premise and allows us to derive the conclusion.

Since there is a New Idea in the Conclusion, (maximizing clients' profits), that idea must be in the correct answer.

The one thing we know from the Evidence that we can swap out in the conclusion is the detail we're told about "older adults" (they're the overlapping idea).

**Goal**

Maybe something like, "If you gear your ads mainly to [the most profitable segment of the market] / [the people who control more personal disposable income than the rest of the population combined], then you'll maximize your clients' profits".

Naturally, they might disguise the correct answer in contrapositive form, and we should wary of illegal reversals / opposites.

A.text: Older people generally have larger incomes and have had longer to accumulate resources than younger people.
A.explanation: This doesn't have any language about "maximizing clients' profits", so it is functionally useless to us.

B.text: No company can maximize its profits unless it markets its products primarily to a population segment that controls most of this nation's personal disposable income.
B.explanation:
This says: max out profits → market mainly to [older people]

But our conclusion is saying: market mainly to [older people] → max out profits

Unless = if it is not the case that. So one way to diagram this is: not marketing to population segment that controls most disposable income → won't maximize profits

Our conclusion is the Opposite of that: do market to population segment that controls most disposable income (i.e. older people) → will maximize profits

C.text: Advertising that is directed toward the wealthiest people is the most effective means for a business to improve the reputation of its products.
C.tag: Unrelated to Goal / Out of Scope = reputation
C.explanation: This doesn't have any language about "maximizing clients' profits", so it is functionally useless to us. Also, the correct answer to Sufficient Assumption will not bring up any new ideas, such as "enhancing the reputation of products".

D.text: No advertising agency that tailors its advertisements mainly to an audience that does not control much of this nation's personal disposable income will maximize its clients' profits.
D.explanation:
This, like (B), is giving us an opposite/reversed version of the conclusion. It's saying: tailor ads mainly to segment of pop that doesn't control much disposable income (i.e. not older adults) → won't maximize clients' profits

Meanwhile, this argument is saying: tailor ads mainly to segment of pop that does control much disposable income (i.e. older adults) → will maximize clients' profits

E.text: Any advertising agency that gears its advertisements mainly to a population segment that controls 50 percent or more of this nation's personal disposable income will maximize its clients' profits.
E.explanation:
We know that "older people" are a population segment that controls more than 50% of the nation's personal disposable income.

There is another modern question (a Principle question about completing the space agency's current project, since the money we'd still have to spend on it is more than the money we've already spent) that uses this same mathematical rephrasing: if one chunk is bigger than the rest combined, then that first chunk is more than 1/2.

Since older people control more than everyone else combined, they have more than half the disposable income. Pick any number for older people, make sure it's more than the combined total for non-older people, and you'll see why it's always more than half.

Older people: 10 billion
not older people: 9 billion
nation's total: 19 billion (older people > 1/2)

So since we know that this language of "pop segment that controls 50% or more" applies to "older people", this rule allows us to say that,

If an ad agency gears its ads mainly to [older people], then it will maximize its clients' profits.

Thus, we've derived the conclusion.

---

standard.breakdownMd:
**Conclusion**

It would be a bad idea if all judges were elected rather than appointed.

**Evidence**

If judges were elected, they'd have to raise funds, which means they'd accept campaign contributions from special interests, which means they'd be likely to run into the same conflicts of interest that politicians run into when they accept contributions.

**Evaluate**

We want a principle that gets us from something we were told in the Evidence about "electing judges", such as
- they'd have to fundraise
- they'd take contributions from special interests
- they'd presumably run into conflicts of interest
and uses that to get us to Conclusion language like "bad idea / should have judges be elected".

**Goal**

If they'd have to fundraise, then electing judges is a bad idea

or

If it would mean that they're taking contributions from special interests, then electing judges shouldn't be done

or (most likely, since this idea was deepest in the chain of Premises)

If it would produce conflicts of interests for judges, then we shouldn't have them be elected.

A.text: If politicians should avoid conflicts of interest, then judges should avoid conflicts of interest as well.
A.explanation:
If this answer simply said "judges should avoid conflicts of interest", then knowing what we were told about electing judges, this would strengthen the idea that judges shouldn't be elected.

But this answer is conditional, so it only has any power if you trigger it.

Can we trigger it? Were we told that politicians should avoid conflicts of interest? Nope. So this answer does nothing for us.

B.text: Special interests should not make offers of campaign contributions to those running for elective office.
B.explanation:
This is a principle that would help us say what special interests should / shouldn't do.

We're looking for a principle that would help us say whether judges should / shouldn't be elected. So this is nowhere close to the right type of wording.

C.text: Judges should be appointed to their positions only if doing so ensures that they will usually be able to avoid conflicts of interest.
C.explanation:
Because "only if" signifies the right side idea, this is saying: should be appointed → appointment ensures usually no conflicts of interest

If we contrapose this, then we have a rule that says, if there usually is conflict of interest, then judges should not be appointed.

That's a bad match for our conclusion, which is "judges should not be elected". The conclusion actually implies we should stick with our current system of appointing judges, so this answer would only help us to disprove the conclusion.

D.text: If judges should be appointed, then it is likely that there are other public offices that should be changed from elected to appointed offices.
D.explanation:
This, structurally, is useless for the same reason (C) was. It's not a rule that helps us to prove "judges should not be elected".

Bizarrely, it's another rule that allows you to prove "judges should not be appointed", which is the opposite of our conclusion.

Remember, that principles (or conditionals) only allow you to prove/conclude the idea to the right of the arrow.

This rule is written: should be appointed → xyz

So we would contrapose it to see its resemblance to the conclusion: ~xyz → should not be appointed

E.text: No public office for which election campaigning would be likely to produce conflicts of interest should be changed from an appointed to an elected office.
E.explanation:
No A's are B = A → ~B

So this rule reads like this: Public office for which election campaigning would be likely to produce conflicts of interest → should not be changed from an appointed office to an elected office

Is judging a public office for which campaigning would be likely to produce conflicts of interest?

Yes. Were they to have to campaign, it is likely that they would accept campaign contributions, which is well-known to lead to conflicts of interest.

Since we can trigger this rule, we can say that "judges should not be changed from appointed to elected officers", which is a great match for our Conclusion.

standard.breakdownMd:
**Evidence**

The machine can make sound (S) only when the outlet is turned on (OTO): S → OTO

Usually when I use the machine, it makes the sound. (Usually, for me, S.)

**Conclusion**

The electric outlet is usually turned on. (Usually, OTO.)

**Evaluate**

Because this has a conditional (only when) and repeating ideas (makes sound / outlet turned on), it's a good contender for looking at the structure.

The flaw seems to be a Sampling one. The conditional logic isn't going backwards. It's just that the author is thinking "if it usually makes the sound for me, then it probably usually makes the sound for everyone."

**Goal**

Look for an argument with a conditional X → Y. Then a premise that's saying, "in my experience, usually X." Then a conclusion that's saying, "thus, usually Y."

A.text: Everyone who has read the new horror novel found the plot disturbing. Indeed, the plot would disturb anyone with a vivid imagination. Therefore, everyone who has read the novel must have a vivid imagination.
A.explanation:
This has a conditional premise: vivid imagination → disturbing

The premise should be saying "in my experience, usually vivid imagination. Thus, usually disturbing."

Instead the premise is about "everyone", when we were looking for a premise that dealt with the author's experience.

And the conclusion should be the outcome of the conditional (disturbing), not vivid imagination. This argument had a different flaw of making a backwards (Necessary vs. Sufficient) move.

B.text: Some people who have read the new horror novel found the plot disturbing. But the plot would not be disturbing to people who lack vivid imaginations. Therefore, some people must have vivid imaginations.
B.explanation:
This has a conditional premise: ~vivid imagination → ~disturbing, i.e. disturbing → vivid imagination

We then have a premise saying, some people found it disturbing.

The conclusion would now need to extrapolate for a broader group that there is vivid imagination.

Instead, the conclusion is safely worded, pertaining only to the "some people" in this evidence. This isn't a Sampling flaw; in fact it's valid logic.

C.text: Many people who have read the new horror novel found the plot disturbing. Undoubtedly, everyone who found the plot disturbing has a vivid imagination. Therefore, many of the people who have read the novel must have vivid imaginations.
C.explanation:
This has a conditional premise: found disturbing → vivid imagination

We have premise saying "many people = disturbing".

The conclusion would now need to extrapolate for a broader group that there is vivid imagination.

Instead, the conclusion is safely worded, pertaining only to the "many people" in this evidence. This isn't a Sampling flaw; in fact it's valid logic, just like (B).

D.text: Most people who have read the new horror novel found the plot disturbing. But the plot cannot disturb anyone who lacks a vivid imagination. Therefore, most people must have vivid imaginations.
D.explanation:
We have a conditional: disturbing → vivid imagination

We have a premise where the trigger is true for some Sample: most [people who have read the novel] found the plot disturbing.

Then we have a conclusion that extrapolates the outcome for a broader group: most [people] have vivid imagination

This ended up straying a bit from our prediction, since it didn't use the first person, but it still went from "trigger is true for a smaller group" to a conclusion that "outcome is true for a larger group".

E.text: Most people who have read the new horror novel found the plot disturbing. But the plot cannot disturb people who lack vivid imaginations. Therefore, most people with vivid imaginations must find the plot disturbing.
E.explanation:
This has a conditional premise: found disturbing → vivid imagination

We have premise saying "most who read novel = disturbing"

The conclusion would now need to extrapolate for a broader group that there is vivid imagination.

Instead, the conclusion talks about "most people with vivid imaginations" and says they found the plot disturbing.

In the original argument, it said "the outcome is true for a broader group".

In this answer, it says "for most people that match the outcome, the trigger is true".

standard.breakdownMd:
**Kira's conclusion**

It's unwise for you to buy that insurance policy.

**Kira's evidence**

It's designed to make the insurance company money. The prices are set to ensure profits.

**Binh's response**

I agree with your evidence (it's designed to make them money), but that doesn't in any way show it's unwise to buy it.

**Evaluate**

When Method questions involve one person responding to another, a lot of what LSAT likes to test is the area of disagreement. Did the 2nd person ..
- disagree with the Conclusion?
- disagree with the Evidence? (this almost never happens)
- disagree with an Assumption?
- just raise a further consideration?

Binh is definitely agreeing with Kira's premise, but he just thinks it's irrelevant when it comes to her conclusion.

He's presumably saying, "All for-profit businesses are designed the same way: the prices are set so that the business makes money. Are you saying it would be unwise for me to buy anything that a for-profit company is selling? It's unwise for me to buy milk, or eggs, because the farming company is going to profit? It's unwise for me to buy Tylenol because the pharmaceutical company is going to profit?"

**Goal**

Look for an answer saying that Binh points out that Kira's evidence, while undeniably true, has no logical force when it comes to supporting the idea that a certain product would be an unwise purchase.

Binh hasn't said as much, but the common sense gist of his response is, "Sure ... isn't that true of any product?" He's sort of saying, "You're acting like this is some negative property specific to this insurance policy, when it's not distinctive at all. It's a feature of every for-profit product."

A.text: suggesting that Kira has overlooked a fact that, although consistent with her premises, is in direct conflict with her conclusion
A.explanation: Binh doesn't present any new facts. He just says, "Yup, your premise is true, but it's garbage in terms of lending any support to your conclusion."

B.text: denying Kira's premises while suggesting that her conclusion, although possibly true, is highly unlikely
B.explanation: Binh explicitly accepts Kira's premises. (in fact, I don't think I've ever seen a correct answer on Method of Response in which the 2nd person denied the truth of the 1st person's evidence)

C.text: arguing that Kira's premises are not only inadequate to prove her conclusion but in fact point strongly toward its being false
C.explanation:
The first half of this is descriptively accurate, but Binh doesn't make any commentary on whether this specific insurance policy would / wouldn't be a wise purchase.

He's only saying that Kira's reason for rejecting it is a completely hollow reason. He doesn't think that her reason actually points in the opposite direction.

D.text: conceding Kira's premises without denying her conclusion, while asserting that the latter does not follow from the former
D.explanation:
Binh does indeed agree to (concede) that Kira's evidence is true. He just says it has no power to influence her conclusion, which means "her conclusion does not follow from her premises".

His final sentence is basically saying this: The fact that [your premises] in no way implies [your conclusion].

And this answer is just saying it inverted: [Your conclusion] in no way follows from [your premises]

E.text: observing that while Kira's premises each independently support her conclusion, the premises themselves are inconsistent with one another
E.explanation:
Binh definitely does not think the premises support her conclusion. He explicitly says that "the mere fact that [your premise] in no way implies [your conclusion]."

Also, saying that premises are inconsistent means that the premises actually contradict each other, which is an incredibly strong accusation that is (almost?) never right.

standard.breakdownMd:
**Conclusion**

The increase in the minimum wage will lead to a decrease in unemployment.

**Evidence**

As people make more, they will spend more on consumer goods, which will lead to an increase in factory jobs to increase production.

**Evaluate**

How could we argue that an increase in the minimum wage will not lead to a decrease in unemployment?

- The first thing that probably comes to mind is that raising the minimum wage raises the overhead costs for businesses that depend on minimum wage employees. They might not be able to handle this uptick in wage expense, and they might have to lay people off, which would increase unemployment.

We should otherwise take each step in the author's causal chain and see if we can push back.

- Will higher min wage lead to more purchases of consumer goods? Maybe not. Maybe the people who start making more money still won't have enough to buy more stuff. Maybe they'll just pay off debts or bills.

- Let's say there were more consumer goods purchased. Will that really lead to the hiring of more people to fill needed factory jobs? Maybe not. Maybe those factories are highly automated so if anything it would just mean more robots.

**Goal**

We need to eliminate four answers that weaken. They will probably either take issue with the predicted implications the author mentioned concerning an increased minimum wage, or they will just offer a new reason why higher minimum wage could increase unemployment (or not reduce it).

A.text: The cost of a minimum-wage increase in Country X will be passed on to consumers in the form of significantly higher prices for consumer goods.
A.explanation: This hurts the connection between higher minimum wage and more purchases of consumer goods. Perhaps the people with higher wages will be eager to spend their extra money, but if the prices of consumer goods go up in general, that will have the effect of decreasing spending on consumer goods.

B.text: Most of the consumer goods sold in Country X are produced outside the country.
B.explanation:
This weakens the connection between higher spending on consumer goods and more domestic jobs being created.

Yes, spending on goods will line the pockets of the manufacturers of these goods, but if they're in other countries mostly, then the new jobs created will be in other countries and won't help to reduce the unemployment in Country X.

C.text: In many factories in Country X, most workers are paid much more than the current minimum wage.
C.explanation:
This has no impact. Someone might think we can weaken the argument by saying, "since most workers make much more than minimum wage, they won't be affected by an increase in the minimum wage, so that weakens the idea that it will quickly lead to a decrease in unemployment."

But this answer is very limited in scope, since it applies to many factories. It's saying that in at least five factories a majority of the workers make well above the current minimum wage.

Okay, does that hurt any part of the story the author is trying to tell? Was she thinking that factory workers were paid at or near the current minimum wage?

No, she's was saying "anyone who DOES make the current minimum wage will have more disposable income when the min wage increase happens, and that extra spending and consumer demand will lead to the creation of factory jobs (that might get paid at any rate, doesn't matter)."

This answer is just kind of a word salad, because in the story the author is telling, the people who make minimum wage are responsible for driving up consumer demand, and the decrease in unemployment will come from the labor demand that creates for factory jobs. But whether factory jobs involve minimum wage is irrelevant.

D.text: The cost to employers of an increase in the minimum wage in Country X will be made up by reductions in the workforce.
D.explanation: This gets at our common sense objection that if we raise minimum wage, some employers won't be able to afford all their employees anymore, so they will lay some off, thereby increasing unemployment.

E.text: Most factories that produce consumer goods in Country X have large surpluses of goods as a result of years of overproduction.
E.explanation:
This attacks the connection between "more consumer goods purchased" and "factories will need to hire more people to make more goods".

It's saying, "Nah, they're good with goods. They've got a large surplus just sitting in a warehouse from years of overproduction."

standard.breakdownMd:
**Principle**

The more someone gets the impression that the person who arranged a group of objects succeeded at what he or she was attempting to do, the more aesthetically pleasing that arrangement is.

**Evaluate / Goal**

This isn't a conditional principle, so we can expect to see some judgments that are more comparative on continuum in nature.

Because of that, it seems like you can take it in either direction.

- If you have the impression the arranger succeeded in their mission → more aesthetically pleasing
- If you have the impression the arranger failed in their mission → less aesthetically pleasing

A.text: The new art installation is very pleasing aesthetically. However, even though it is not apparent to viewers, the artist did not intend the wooden panels to be arranged the way they in fact are. So the panels should be rearranged to reflect the artist's intention.
A.explanation: The viewers don't realize that the arranger didn't accomplish their goal, but this principle needs the viewers to know that the arranger did accomplish their goal. Otherwise we shouldn't be labeling it very aesthetically pleasing.

B.text: The wooden panels in the art installation probably are not arranged in the way that the artist wanted them arranged, for the installation is less aesthetically pleasing than other installations.
B.explanation:
I don't hate this one, but the Conclusion / Premise should probably be swapped. We would use the criterion of "this arrangement gives the clear impression that the arranger succeeded at their intent, thus aesthetically pleasing".

But maybe more importantly is that this talks about whether or not the artist succeeded, whereas what we need to hear about is whether the arrangement "gives the impression" that the artist succeeded.

C.text: The arrangement of wooden panels in the art installation is likely to give the impression that the artist who arranged them did not quite succeed at what she was attempting to do, for the arrangement is almost, but not quite, symmetrical.
C.explanation: This clarifies whether or not the impression of success was given off, but this doesn't have anything about how aesthetically pleasing the art is / isn't.

D.text: The art installation would be more aesthetically pleasing if the wooden panels in it were arranged more symmetrically, for then it would seem more like the artist had gotten the panels arranged the way she wanted.
D.explanation: This clearly connects the idea of "giving off the impression of successful attempt" with "more aesthetically pleasing".

E.text: The artist could make the arrangement of wooden panels in the art installation more aesthetically pleasing by making it less symmetrical, for then it would give less of an impression that every aspect of the arrangement was fully planned.
E.explanation:
This is saying "by making this look less fully planned (less intentional / less like a successful execution of the arranger's vision)", it will be "more aesthetically pleasing".

That has the principle backwards.

standard.breakdownMd:
**Conclusion**

Having a larger size is a better defense against the lake's predators than is armor.

**Evidence**

The lake stickleback has virtually no armor, while the ocean stickleback is covered with armor to protect them from their predators.

The armor limits the speed of a stickleback's growth.

**Evaluate**

Yikes. This is a tough one to organize. I would use the typical Curious Fact / Explanation template that is so common on Strengthen and Weaken.

Curious Fact: how come the lake stickleback has no armor, while the ocean stickleback does have armor?

Author's Story: for the sake of protection against the lake's predators, the stickleback would be better off being large than having armor, and having armor slows a stickleback's growth. So natural selection resulted in larger, armorless stickleback in lakes.

We should then think our two questions for this template:
1. is there some OTHER WAY we could explain this curious fact?
2. how plausible is the AUTHOR'S WAY of explaining it?

1. Maybe the armor is made from salt and other minerals that would be found in an ocean but not in a freshwater lake. Perhaps the lake just doesn't have the same raw materials the ocean has that would allow a stickleback to biologically construct the typical armor. Maybe the armor would have been useful for predators, but large size offers some other advantage (better success mating?)

2. To believe the author's story, I definitely need to assume a difference between the ocean predators and the lake predators. I'm not sure what that difference would be, but it should be where armor is a better defense against the ocean attackers and large size is better against the lake attackers. To weaken the argument, we could hear an answer saying that "the lake stickleback and the ocean stickleback have similar predators".

**Goal**

Look for an answer that suggests a different way to explain why the lake stickleback lack armor, or for an answer that undermines the plausibility that stickleback are better off with largeness than with armor, when it comes to fending off the lake's predators.

A.text: Sticklebacks with armor are unable to swim as fast, making them most vulnerable to fast-moving predators.
A.explanation: We don't know whether the ocean or the lake has faster predators, so there's no way to apply this new information to the distinction we're trying to explain.

B.text: Having a larger size is an important factor in whether lake stickleback, but not ocean stickleback, survive cold winters.
B.explanation:
Here is the Alternate Explanation answer we expect, when we're Weakening a Curious Fact / Explanation type argument.

The lake stickleback aren't larger because that helps them more against the lake's predators, they're larger because that helps them survive cold winters.

Importantly, this alternate cause has to be something that only applies to the lake stickleback, so we're happy to see that "but not ocean stickleback" distinguisher in this answer.

C.text: Unlike ocean stickleback, the lake stickleback are more often preyed upon by predatory insects than by larger fish.
C.explanation:
The author's explanation assumes a difference between the lake stickleback's predators and the ocean stickleback's predators. This answer establishes that there is a difference. In that sense, it strengthens the plausibility of the author's hypothesis.

But the author wasn't just assuming any ol' difference. She's assuming that armor works better against ocean predators and size works better against lake predators.

This answer suggests that ocean predators tend to be larger fish, whereas lake predators tend to be predatory insects. Does our common sense say that armor works better when you're being attacked by larger fish, but size works better if you're being attacked by predatory insects?

People's answers to that question are pretty divergent. I've heard students (and other LSAT teachers) make the case that you'd rather have armor against predatory insects, and I've heard students/teachers make the case that you'd rather have size against predatory insects.

The fact that we test takers don't agree about what impact it has to be bigger vs. possess armor, in regards to predatory insects, suggests that there isn't a strong common sense take on the impact of this answer.

Meanwhile, the correct answer unequivocally weakens by showing that there's an alternate explanation for why the lake stickleback would "want to evolve" to be larger.

D.text: Both ocean stickleback and lake stickleback feed primarily on the same types of foods.
D.explanation:
This would rule out any alternate story that relates to different eating needs. It's possible that lake stickleback evolved to be larger because that helped them eat lake-food.

But this rules out that possibility. Since the author thinks that "different predators" are the causal difference-maker, when it comes to why the lake stickleback lacks armor and the ocean stickleback has armor, her argument is strengthened by controlling for any other potential causal difference-maker.

If you want to argue that "different predators" is why these two species are different, you want to believe that the difference is not due to different food supply, different mating habits, different habitat demands, etc.

E.text: Sticklebacks originated in the ocean but began populating freshwater lakes and streams following the last ice age.
E.explanation:
Since the author is positing an evolutionary adaptation to the lake, the author needs to assume that the stickleback has been in the lake long enough for natural selection to take its slow effect.

So, if anything, establishing that the stickleback diverged into ocean and lake varieties a long, long time ago might strengthen the argument by making it seem like the two stickleback populations have been apart for long enough that they plausibly could have evolved different traits.

standard.breakdownMd:
- **Given that...:** A company produced a small car that costs much less—but is also much less safe—than any car previously available.
- **How can it be that...:** Most customers of the new car increased their safety on the roads by buying it.
- **Evaluate / Goal:** We're told that this small car is much less safe when compared to other cars, which leads us to believe that the customers of the new car would decrease their safety by driving it. Why have most customers increased their safety?

  Perhaps people who buy this car tend to do something that increases their safety on the roads. Maybe they drive more carefully because they know the car is much less safe.

  We're also told that the car costs much less, so maybe the drivers are doing something with the money they save which increases their safety. Maybe they buy tires more often, so they're less likely to have an accident caused by worn-out tires.

  A correct answer could suggest one of these possibilities, or perhaps some other factor that helps the drivers of these cars increase their safety on the roads.

A.text: The company surveyed potential customers and discovered that most of them were more concerned about cost than about safety.
A.explanation: If potential customers are more concerned about cost than safety, this doesn't explain how they increase their safety on the roads. If anything, it indicates that they would be less safe.

B.text: The company could significantly increase the car's safety without dramatically increasing its production cost.
B.explanation: Something that the company "could" do doesn't impact what has already happened. The stimulus indicates that customers have already increased their safety by buying the car.

C.text: Most people who bought the new car were probably unaware that it is much less safe than other cars.
C.explanation: It's not clear how this impacts the apparent paradox of customers increasing their safety by buying this car. If anything, being unaware of the safety issue would make them less likely to drive more carefully, which would be the opposite of what we're looking for.

D.text: Many households that previously could afford only one car can now afford two.
D.explanation:
This would seem to mean that it's easier for someone to buy one of these cars, even if they already have a car. It's not clear how that would help people who own the new car increase their safety.

This could also mean that families are buying more than one of these rolling death traps, which might be the opposite of what we're looking for, if anything.

E.text: Most people who bought the new car previously travelled by bicycle or motorcycle, which are less safe than the new car.
E.explanation:
The stimulus compares the new small car to "any car previously available," but doesn't state how safe the new car is compared to other forms of transportation, like riding a bicycle or motorcycle. If this answer choice is true, people who buy the new car are safer because they're no longer using more dangerous methods of transportation. Wear your helmets, kids.

standard.breakdownMd:
- **Conclusion (This proves that):** Eating bread and meat in the same meal is unhealthy.
- **Evidence:** I used to eat fast food burgers almost every day, until I read that eating bread and meat in the same meal interferes with digestion.

  So now I'm eating lean meats, fruits, and vegetables and I feel much better and my cholesterol level and blood pressure are lower.
- **Evaluate:** The author is trying to solve the causal mystery of why he feels better on his new diet, so we can use an Explain Curious Fact mindset.

  Curious Fact ... why do I feel better and have lower cholesterol and blood pressure since I switched from daily fast food burgers to a diet of lean meats, fruits, and vegetables?

  Author's Explanation ... It's because I was eating bread and meat in the same meal, which supposedly interferes with digestion, (and thus made me feel worse and caused higher cholesterol and blood pressure)

  When we see this template arise on Flaw, the correct answer is almost always complaining that the author has failed to consider some Alternate Explanation for the curious fact. What could be a different explanation for why he's doing better on the new diet?

  We could say, "It's not because you were combining bread and meat in the same meal. It's because you were eating fast-food almost every day. That stuff is garbage for you, nutritionally."

  We could also say, "the improvement isn't because you stopped combining bread and meat. It's because you started eating really healthy things like fruits and vegetables."
- **Goal:** Look for an answer complaining that this author has failed to rule out some alternate explanation for his improved condition (or one complaining that this hypothesis isn't a plausible one, since improved digestion might have anything to do with lower cholesterol and blood pressure).

A.text: treats a statement as established fact merely because a self-appointed expert has asserted it
A.explanation:
This is referencing one of the 10 famous flaws, Inappropriate Appeal to a Dubious Expert.

There is no self-appointed expert mentioned. The author definitely acted on an idea she read somewhere, but she never talks about someone who considers themselves an expert and whose opinion she treats as fact.

B.text: draws a conclusion that merely restates a premise offered in support of it
B.explanation:
This is referencing one of the 10 famous flaws, Circular reasoning, in which a premise restates the conclusion or presumes its truth. These answers are almost always wrong.

The conclusion is that "eating bread and meat in the same meal is unhealthy", and there is definitely not a premise that restates that claim ("interferes with digestion" ≠ "is unhealthy").

C.text: treats a condition that must occur in order for an effect to occur as a condition that would ensure that the effect occurs
C.explanation:
This is referencing the most common of the 10 famous flaws, Necessary vs. Sufficient, in which an author presents a conditional logic premise and then applies it in some illegal reversed or negated fashion.

There was no conditional logic premise, so she can't be guilty of an illegal reversal or negation.

D.text: concludes that one part of a change was responsible for an effect without ruling out the possibility that other parts of that change were responsible
D.explanation:
The author concludes that "discontinuing having bread and meat in the same meal" is why she feels better and has lower cholesterol and BP.

Meanwhile, it's possible that splitting up bread and meat was not the change that is really responsible for the improved condition.

Maybe it was the change of "not eating fast food almost every day". Maybe it was the change of "eating fruits and veggies".

This argument is dealing with another of the 10 famous flaws, Causal Overconfidence, in which the author overconfidently concludes one causal explanation for a curious fact while failing to consider other possible explanations.

E.text: concludes that making a dietary change improved the health of a particular person simply because that change results in improved health for most people
E.explanation:
The author does conclude that making the dietary change of splitting up bread and meat improved their particular health.

But she does not conclude this on the basis of evidence that said, "most people who stop combining bread and meat end up with improved health".

---

standard.breakdownMd:
- **Statements:**

```
conditional (only if)

Newly formed neurons              Can't help
aren't of the type that's    →    to heal an
most common in the area           injured brain
```

  When it comes to the striatum, the most common type of neuron in the area is the midsized spiny neuron. But newly formed neurons there aren't of that type.
- **Evaluate:** It seems like this is a classic Must Be True where they provide us with a conditional rule and then test our Contrapositive Logic abilities, in applying it to some fact.

  For example, if we were told "Only blond firemen appeared in the calendar" and then told "Mario is a brunette", then we can infer that "Mario did not appear in the calendar".

  Here, we were told that "only neurons that match the most common local type can help heal an injured brain" and then told "in the striatum, the new neurons never match the most common local type (midsized spiny)".
- **Goal:** Thus, we should be able to infer something like, "when it comes to the striatum, newly formed neurons never help to heal an injured brain".

A.text: Newly formed neurons sometimes develop into midsized spiny neurons in areas of the brain other than the striatum.
A.tag: Out of Scope: other than the striatum
A.explanation:
We have no idea if newly formed neurons do become midsized spiny neurons anywhere. It's possible they just never become midsized spiny neurons.

This answer is trying to trap people into thinking that "the opposite of what we said applies in other contexts".

Like if the passage said, "Jane is very polite at church", this answer would be baiting people into thinking, "so does that mean Jane is very impolite when she's not at church"? That's never a legal inference.

We can affirm that "black lives matter" without implying that "non-black lives don't matter".

B.text: Newly formed neurons are commonly found in injured areas of the brain shortly after the injury occurs.
B.tag: Out of Scope: shortly after injury
B.explanation: We don't have any time-sensitive information about when newly formed neurons come on the scene. This is Must Be True, so we can't fabricate or speculate. We're just trying to derive truisms based on what we were told.

C.text: Midsized spiny neurons are not the most common type of neuron in any part of the brain other than the striatum.
C.tag: Too Strong: any part / Out of Scope: outside striatum
C.explanation:
Just like (A), we have no information whatsoever about what goes on outside the striatum. Just because midsized spiny are the most common within the striatum doesn't mean that the opposite is true outside the striatum.

Just because Jane is polite at church doesn't mean she's impolite when she's not at church. She might just be polite!

D.text: In cases of injury to the striatum, newly formed neurons will not help to heal the injury.
D.explanation:
As we predicted, by applying the conditional rule in the first sentence to the facts provided in the second sentence, we can derive that newly formed neurons won't help to heal an injury to the striatum.

Newly formed neurons only help heal if they match the most common local type of neuron, and newly formed neurons in the striatum will never match the most common local type of neuron in the striatum.

E.text: In most cases of brain injury, newly formed neurons do not help to heal the injury.
E.explanation:
We only know about the case of the striatum. This information doesn't allow us to derive anything about other cases of brain injury.

---

standard.breakdownMd:
- **Conclusion:** Thompson's article is intriguing but ultimately puzzling.
- **Evidence:** In one scene, he says that a character's furrowed brow indicates inner turmoil and anxiety.

  Later, he says this same character in the same scene is a "self-identified agent", but he begins the article by saying that a "self-identified agent" is incapable of having misgivings or anxiety.
- **Evaluate:** Leona is basically saying that this article contradicts itself.

```

~standard → ~replace passwords
```

```
~standard → ~replace passwords
~standard
Therefore, ~replace passwords
```

  So, a correct answer might state that other security options are not standard on most computers.

  There's also a second path to the conclusion. The evidence states that other options are significantly more expensive to employ. The conclusion follows logically if we assume:

```
more $ → ~replace passwords
```

```
significantly more expensive.                            more $

This answer states that more expensive options will
not become standard on most computers.                   more $ → ~standard

The evidence already states that, if other options do
not become standard on most computers, they will not
replace passwords.                                       ~standard → ~replace

This allows us to conclude that these other options
will not replace passwords.                              ~replace
```

standard.breakdownMd:
- **Conclusion:** This refutes those who claim that would-be drunk drivers will not be deterred by the prospect of severe penalties.

  rephrase: Would-be drunk drivers will be deterred by the prospect of severe penalties.
- **Evidence:** In countries with the most severe penalties for drunk driving, a smaller percentage of drivers have traffic accidents involving alcohol.
- **Evaluate:** Any time the evidence includes a statistic, study, artifact, or experiment, it's likely that the author's conclusion will announce or assume some causal interpretation of that evidence. We use our Explain Curious Fact mindset for these.

  Curious Fact .... why is there a correlation between countries with severe penalties for drunk driving and lower % of drivers having traffic accidents involving alcohol?

  Author's Explanation ... the harsh penalties scare citizens out of drunk driving.

  As always, we consider the two pressure points of such an argument:
  1. Alternate Explanations for the curious fact
  2. the plausibility of the author's explanation

  Whenever the author presents a correlation between X and Y and concludes/assumes that X causes Y, we reflexively consider two possible alternate explanations:
  - Reverse Cause (maybe Y causes X)
  - 3rd Factor (maybe X and Y are both connected to some other factor Z)

  Here, it doesn't make much sense to say that "Having a lower percentage of drivers involved in alcohol related accidents led to having more severe penalties for drunk driving". So, if we're going to weaken via Alternate Explanation, it will probably be a 3rd factor. For example, maybe the countries with the most severe penalties for drunk driving also happen to have cities that are more walkable / public transportation that is more usable.

  We could say, "the low % of alcohol accidents isn't because of the severe penalties. It's because people can walk or take the bus/train, rather than drive home."
- **Goal:** It's more common to weaken with an Alternate Explanation, so we'll primarily look for that, but we might otherwise see a correct answer that hurts the plausibility of the idea that "severe penalties are discouraging people from otherwise drunk driving" (f.e. maybe citizens have no idea what the penalties are for drunk driving).

A.text: The countries with the largest populations do not have severe penalties for driving while intoxicated.
A.explanation:
The raw number of population size makes no difference in this argument, because the statistic we're examining is talking about the percentage of drivers involved in alcohol related accidents.

These countries with unusually low %'s of drivers involved in alcohol related accidents could be among the most populous countries, the least populous, or both.

B.text: Very severe penalties against driving while intoxicated are in effect only in countries in which alcohol use is rare.
B.explanation:
This identifies a 3rd Factor Alternate Explanation.

The author thinks that alcohol related traffic accidents are low because the severe penalties act as a deterrent to keep people from drunk driving.

This answer allows us to say, "Nah, the reason you see less alcohol-related accidents in this country isn't because the drunk driving laws are severe; it's just because alcohol use is very rare."

There might be countries where the dominant religion heavily discourages drinking. And the laws of that country put very severe penalties against drunk driving, but really what's keeping there from being alcohol-related accidents is that people there don't drink (for religious reasons).

This answer is technically a conditional. If we think it would be useful, we would think to ourselves about how the contrapositive sounds:

```
If alcohol use in a       →    then there are not severe
country is common              penalties for drunk driving
```

This makes it seem like the effect of "severe penalties" on drunk driving is never really getting tested. We wouldn't test the effectiveness of a mosquito repellant in an area where mosquitoes were rare.

If there were some rule like, "Wherever mosquitoes are common, you won't find this mosquito repellant", then we really have no way to judge whether the repellant actually discourages mosquitoes.

C.text: The higher a country's speed limits, the more frequent traffic accidents tend to be in that country.
C.explanation:
This answer is impossible to relate to the conversation at hand, because it talks about speed limits and traffic accidents (in general, not specifically alcohol-related ones).

We'd have no way to connect this information to the topic at hand.

Do countries with severe penalties for drunk driving have higher speed limits than average? Lower? Moderate? We have no idea.

Are the traffic accidents alluded to in this answer alcohol-related? We have no idea.

D.text: Only a relatively small minority of those who drive while intoxicated are actually apprehended while doing so.
D.explanation:
This somewhat weakens the plausibility of the author's explanation. She is arguing that severe penalties for drunk driving deter some drunk people from driving.

If, however, those drunk people knew that only a small minority of drunk drivers are ever caught in the act, they would have less to fear and thus be less deterred from drunk driving.

However, this answer isn't clarifying whether drunk people who are considering drunk driving are actually aware that only a small minority of drunk drivers get caught. They might not realize they have a good chance of not being apprehended.

Furthermore, "only a relatively small minority" could still be like 15% of drunk drivers. If I told you, "there's only a 1 in 6 chance you'll get caught if you drive home drunk, but if you do, you know that the severe penalty is 20 years in jail", would you be deterred? Or would you accept those odds?

Chances are, if we're scared of the stiff penalty of getting caught, we will still be somewhat nervous about doing something even if we stand a pretty good chance of getting away with it.

Ultimately, this weakens somewhat, but it doesn't have the dramatic weakening effect that the correct answer has.

E.text: All countries impose severer penalties on those who cause accidents while driving intoxicated than on those who are merely apprehended while driving intoxicated.
E.explanation:
Since this applies to all countries, it really won't inform any judgments we're hoping to make about whether countries with the most severe penalties are thereby deterring people from driving drunk.
